There is no melting data known by the authors that support a liquidus that rises as quickly as those shown by Pfeil (1950) or Garg and Ackermann (1977). Rest et al. (2006) and perhaps Zhang et al. (2010) indicate an initial melting point depression at low Mo content, with the phase construction appearing to exhibit a positive azeotrope at ∼3 wt.% Mo. This is thermodynamically possible but the only data that supports such a reaction are given by Ahmann, though the original phase diagram construction suggests that such a trend was not accepted by the authors as it is not generally accepted today. This type of trend may instead indicate impurity levels which introduce an observable eutectic (or other reaction type) or may be used to indicate the relative error to be expected in the measurements. All other investigations have concluded that the liquidus and solidus monotonically increase with increasing Mo before terminating at the peritectic temperature (Mardon et al. 1959; English 1961; Brewer 1980; Hiroaki Okamoto and Massalski 1990; Berche et al. 2011; H. Okamoto 2012; IAEA 2021). Unfortunately Brewer (1980) reports a topologically impossible set of phase boundaries in the form of crossing solidus and liquidus lines. It is assumed that this is a result of misreported equations, but the figure that accompanies the text also shows the impossibility. During the earliest stages of writing this current report, a new IAEA Techdoc was released which addressed the U-Mo phase diagram (IAEA 2021), making it the most recent review of existing work and data. That document’s authors purposefully attempt to remain tied as closely as possible to the experimentally defined phase boundaries. It should be reiterated that little or no direct interrogation of the solidus and liquidus has been formally produced since 1977. H. Okamoto (2012) had been until 2021, the most up-to-date edited phase diagram and for the U-rich liquidus and solidus appears to have relied heavily on the work of Berchè. The work of Berchè and reassessment of the temperature by Okamoto represented a significant change as compared to previous authors and review diagrams in that the peritectic temperature was revised upward.
